opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons, and they stack on top of each other.

The first is that the ingredients are already on the table. If you look back at what made the GPT moment happen for language, it wasn't one magic trick. It was a combination: a simple, scalable objective like next-token prediction, a huge amount of naturally occurring data, the Transformer architecture, and enough compute to push scaling far enough that emergent abilities showed up. For multimodality, most of those pieces already exist. We have the architectures, we have the engineering experience of training very large models, we know how to build the data pipelines and the infrastructure. In the language era, people had to discover all of that from scratch. Now the whole field has gone through that learning curve once, so the second time is much faster.

The second reason is that the missing piece is now relatively well-defined. In my view, the core problem with vision so far is that we haven't found a training paradigm that gives images the same "closed loop" that next-token prediction gives text. In language, generation and understanding are naturally unified: if you can predict the next word well, you have to understand the context. In vision, understanding and generation have mostly been separate tracks. We have models that understand images by aligning them to text, and we have diffusion models that generate beautiful images, but the generation doesn't really feed back into understanding, and the understanding doesn't really make generation smarter. When a problem is that clearly framed, a lot of very smart people around the world attack it at once, and that tends to compress the timeline.

The third reason is that there are already signals. When you look at recent work on unified models, on combining autoregressive and diffusion approaches, on video models, and on letting models reason over images in a chain of thought, you start to see glimmers of the behavior you'd expect: models that can manipulate visual content step by step, that show some generalization they weren't explicitly trained for. It's not yet the full GPT-3 or ChatGPT moment for vision, but it feels similar to the period just before those moments in language, when the signals were there but scaled up hadn't happened yet.

And finally, the incentives and the resources are enormous. Compute, talent, and capital are all concentrated on this direction now. Ten years ago a breakthrough might sit in a paper for a while before anyone scaled it. Today, once someone shows a recipe that works, it gets reproduced and scaled within months.

So I'm not saying it's trivial. There are still real open questions, especially about what the right "next token" for vision is, and how to get data that carries the kind of rich reasoning that text naturally contains. But because the infrastructure, the experience, and the attention are all already there, I believe once the key insight clicks, things will move very quickly. It could be a matter of one or two years rather than a decade.

r001.rationale: The response says the key ingredients for multimodality already exist—including architectures, large-model training experience, data pipelines, and infrastructure—and presents that readiness as a reason progress will be faster.

fable-5.1.text:
Mainly because I think we've already seen this pattern once. Look at how the language side developed: GPT-3 came out in 2020, and within a couple of years the whole community had converged on roughly the same recipe, so by the time ChatGPT appeared, everyone could follow pretty quickly. The hard part was not the engineering, it was knowing that the direction was right. Once OpenAI showed that scaling plus next-token prediction works, that uncertainty disappeared, and the rest became a matter of compute and execution.

Multimodal is in a similar position now. The basic ingredients are mostly on the table. We have strong language models as the backbone. We have vision encoders that work. We have a lot of evidence that if you tokenize images, audio, or video into a shared sequence and train on enough data, the model picks up cross-modal abilities for free. The open questions are more about the details: how to do the visual tokenizer well, how to balance understanding and generation, how to get the data pipeline to scale. Those are real problems, but they are the kind of problems the field is very good at grinding through once people agree on the goal.

The other thing is that the amount of talent and money pointed at this is much larger than it was for language in 2020. Back then a handful of labs believed in it. Now almost every major lab, and a lot of startups, are racing toward the same target. When that many strong teams are working on a problem whose direction is already fairly clear, I don't think it takes long. My guess is we see something that feels like a GPT-3 moment for multimodal within a year or two, and the jump from there to a really usable product will be faster than it was for text.

r001.rationale: The response says the basic multimodal ingredients are mostly in place—strong language models, working vision encoders, and evidence for shared-sequence training—and links that readiness to rapid progress.

astra-6.text:
I think progress will be quick because the different modalities can reinforce each other. Language gives you a way to describe and reason about what’s in an image or a video, while images and video give language more grounding. So improvements in one area can help the others.

You also don’t have to start from scratch. You can build on the capabilities of existing models and work on getting them to learn together. That doesn’t mean every challenge is solved—understanding timing, motion, and the relationship between sound and vision is still difficult—but there’s a clear path to making useful progress.

r001.rationale: The response cites cross-modal reinforcement and building on existing models as reasons for quick progress, but does not clearly attribute that progress to prerequisite technologies being ready.

sol-6.1.text: I think progress will be quick because the different modalities can reinforce one another. Language gives you a way to describe and reason about what’s in an image or a video, while visual and audio inputs give the model information that text alone can’t provide. We’re also building on an existing foundation, so we don’t have to start from scratch for each modality. That makes me optimistic, although getting everything to work together reliably is still a substantial challenge.

r001.rationale: The response attributes quick progress to modalities reinforcing one another and an existing foundation, but it does not say the prerequisite technologies appear ready.
